```{r setup, include = FALSE}
  collapse = TRUE,

library(AlphaSimR)
```

## Introduction

Truncation selection takes the best individuals and nothing else into
account. Relatives tend to be among the best together, so a population
under truncation selection is soon descended from a few families, and
the genetic variance that future gain depends on is lost quickly
[@robertson1961Inbreeding]. The
[Selection](Selection.html) article shows this happening.

Optimal contribution selection [@meuwissen1997Maximizing] makes the
trade-off explicit: it maximizes the merit of the selected individuals
subject to a limit on the rate at which inbreeding, or equivalently
fixation, increases. @woolliams2015Genetic review the theory. Full
optimal contribution selection chooses how many offspring each
candidate should have.

`selectOC` implements an approximation in which every selected
individual contributes equally. It answers a narrower but common
question, *which* individuals to keep, while leaving the crossing plan to
you. This article explains what it restricts, shows it in a simulation,
and covers measuring the restriction with markers or with the pedigree.

## What is restricted

`selectOC` restricts the **expected fixation** of the gametes the
selected individuals will supply. With genotypes at a SNP chip, the
expected fixation of a set of individuals is
$$F = \frac{1}{m}\sum_j (2\bar{p}_j - 1)^2 = 1 - \frac{H}{H_{max}},$$
where $\bar{p}_j$ is the frequency of an allele at locus $j$ among their
gametes, $H$ the mean expected heterozygosity and $H_{max} = 0.5$ its
largest possible value. For diploids $F$ equals the average coancestry of
the selected individuals, measured relative to a base population with
allele frequencies of 0.5.

The target is set by `inbrTarget` and `inbrType`. The default,
`inbrType = "relative"` with `inbrTarget = 0.01`, allows the expected
fixation to rise by 1% of the remaining heterozygosity each generation,
$\Delta F = 0.01$. Because $\Delta F = 1/(kN_e)$ for ploidy $k$, this
corresponds to an effective population size of 50 for a diploid. With
`inbrType = "absolute"`, `inbrTarget` is instead the largest allowed
value of $F$ itself, which is useful when the candidates were already
preselected and their own fixation is not a sensible reference.

## A first look

The example uses `runMacs` founders, so that markers and QTL are in
linkage disequilibrium as they would be in a real population, and tracks
the pedigree from the start, which the pedigree version of the method
needs.

```{r}
set.seed(1997)

founderPop = runMacs(nInd = 200, nChr = 10, segSites = 300)

SP = SimParam$new(founderPop)
```
```{r include=FALSE}
SP$nThreads = 1L
```
```{r}
SP$setTrackPed(TRUE)
SP$restrSegSites(minQtlPerChr = 50, minSnpPerChr = 200)
SP$addTraitA(nQtlPerChr = 50)
SP$addSnpChip(nSnpPerChr = 200)
SP$setVarE(h2 = 0.3)

basePop = newPop(founderPop, simParam = SP)
pop = randCross(basePop, nCrosses = 40, nProgeny = 5, simParam = SP)
```

Selecting 40 parents from 40 families of five, first by truncation and
then by `selectOC`:

```{r}
nParents = 40
family = function(x) paste(x@mother, x@father)

truncated = selectInd(pop, nInd = nParents, simParam = SP)
restricted = selectOC(pop, nInd = nParents, simParam = SP)
```

`selectOC` reports the value of the Lagrange multiplier $\kappa$ it
settled on, the expected fixation achieved, the target, and the
expected fixation of the whole population. Here $\kappa$ is zero: the
40 best phenotypes already come from enough families to meet the
default target, and when that happens the result is ordinary truncation
selection. A tighter target, half the default, makes the restriction
bind:

```{r}
tighter = selectOC(pop, nInd = nParents, inbrTarget = 0.005,
                   simParam = SP)
```

Comparing the three sets:

```{r}
fixation = function(x){
  p = colMeans(pullSnpGeno(x, simParam = SP)) / 2
  mean((2 * p - 1)^2)
}

round(rbind(
  truncation = c(meanG = unname(meanG(truncated)[1]), F = fixation(truncated),
                 families = length(unique(family(truncated)))),
  OCS = c(meanG = unname(meanG(restricted)[1]), F = fixation(restricted),
          families = length(unique(family(restricted)))),
  tighter = c(meanG = unname(meanG(tighter)[1]), F = fixation(tighter),
              families = length(unique(family(tighter))))
), 4)
```

At the default target the two sets are the same. With the tighter
target, `selectOC` gives up a little merit to draw its parents from more
families and bring the expected fixation under the target. The fixation
values are large, around 0.45, because they are measured relative to
allele frequencies of 0.5, and few loci in a real or `runMacs` population
are at 0.5. What the restriction controls is the change from one
generation to the next.

## Using the selected individuals

The restriction holds only if the selected individuals are used as it
assumes: each contributes equally to the next generation. `randCross`
samples crosses at random, so parents get unequal numbers of progeny by
chance. A crossing plan that uses every parent equally avoids that; a
circle, in which each parent is crossed with the next, is the simplest:

```{r}
circle = function(n) cbind(1:n, c(2:n, 1))

progeny = makeCross(restricted, crossPlan = circle(nParents),
                    nProgeny = 5, simParam = SP)
table(table(c(progeny@mother, progeny@father)))
```

Every parent appears in two crosses of five progeny, so each contributes
ten gametes. `selectCross` with `restrInbr = TRUE` makes the same
selection and then crosses at random, which is convenient but only
approximately equal.

## Over many generations

The real test is what happens over many generations. The simulation
below runs three strategies for 20 generations from the same population,
each selecting 40 parents on phenotype and crossing them in a circle:

- **truncation**: the best 40 phenotypes;
- **OCS, markers**: `selectOC` with the default target, measured at the
  SNP chip;
- **OCS, pedigree**: `selectOC` with the same target, measured with the
  pedigree (`usePed = TRUE`).

The fixation at the SNP chip and the average pedigree inbreeding of each
generation are recorded, along with the mean genetic value and the genic
variance.

```{r}
runStrategy = function(strategy, nGen = 20){
  x = pop
  out = NULL
  for(gen in 0:nGen){
    out = rbind(out, data.frame(
      generation = gen,
      meanG = meanG(x)[1],
      genicVarA = genicVarA(x, simParam = SP)[1],
      fixation = fixation(x),
      pedigreeF = mean(pedigreeInbreeding(x, simParam = SP))))
    if(gen == nGen) break
    parents = switch(strategy,
      truncation = selectInd(x, nInd = nParents, simParam = SP),
      markers = suppressMessages(
        selectOC(x, nInd = nParents, simParam = SP)),
      pedigree = suppressMessages(
        selectOC(x, nInd = nParents, usePed = TRUE, simParam = SP)))
    x = makeCross(parents, crossPlan = circle(nParents), nProgeny = 5,
                  simParam = SP)
  }
  out
}

strategies = c("truncation", "markers", "pedigree")
results = lapply(strategies, runStrategy)
names(results) = strategies
```

```{r fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
cols = c("black", "red", "blue")
panel = function(column, label){
  plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, 20),
       ylim = range(sapply(results, `[[`, column)),
       xlab = "Generation", ylab = label)
  for(i in seq_along(results)){
    lines(results[[i]]$generation, results[[i]][[column]],
          col = cols[i], lwd = 2)
  }
}
panel("meanG", "Mean genetic value")
legend("topleft", legend = strategies, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
panel("genicVarA", "Genic additive variance")
panel("fixation", "Fixation at the SNP chip")
panel("pedigreeF", "Pedigree inbreeding")
```

The rate of increase per generation, relative to what remains, can be
compared with the target of 0.01:

```{r}
rate = function(f){
  n = length(f)
  mean((f[-1] - f[-n]) / (1 - f[-n]))
}

round(sapply(results, function(x){
  c(meanG = x$meanG[nrow(x)],
    genicVarA = x$genicVarA[nrow(x)],
    rateFixation = rate(x$fixation),
    ratePedigreeF = rate(x$pedigreeF))
}), 4)
```

Each version of `selectOC` holds the rate it measures close to the
target of 0.01: the marker version for fixation at the SNP chip, and the
pedigree version for pedigree inbreeding. Truncation exceeds the target
on both measures. Neither restriction controls the other's measure
exactly, as @sonesson2012Genomic also found. The pedigree version let fixation at the SNP chip rise faster
than truncation did, because the pedigree cannot see which alleles
individuals carry, and the marker version let pedigree inbreeding rise
somewhat above the target.

Both restricted strategies also made more gain than truncation over 20
generations in this run. That is not guaranteed: restricting inbreeding
costs gain in the short term, and the return comes from the variance it
preserves. Over the 20 generations here the genic variance differed
little between the strategies, so the ranking of gains is not a robust
result of this single run.

A single run is one realization of a random process, and these
strategies differ by amounts comparable to the variation between runs.
A real comparison repeats each strategy many times.

## Markers or pedigree

The two ways of measuring the restriction behave differently.

With **markers**, the kinship of two candidates is estimated from the
genotypes they actually carry. The method can therefore balance allele
frequencies, keeping candidates whose alleles are rare among the others
selected, and it sees the Mendelian sampling that makes one sib differ
from another [@daetwyler2007Inbreeding].

With the **pedigree**, kinship is taken from `pedigreeA`, relative to the
founders of the simulation, and the pedigree knows only who descends
from whom. Full sibs are related alike to everyone else, so the
restriction works by spreading selection across families, and sibs are
chosen between on merit. Because of this, the individuals are chosen one
at a time with the pedigree, each penalized for its relationships to the
ones already taken; the marker version penalizes each candidate against
the allele frequencies of the whole selected set. The help page of
`selectOC` gives both methods in full.

A few consequences:

- The pedigree version needs the pedigree tracked from the start of the
  simulation, with `SP$setTrackPed(TRUE)` before the first population.
- Its measure is inbreeding relative to the founders, which is zero at
  the start, while the marker measure is fixation relative to allele
  frequencies of 0.5, which is not. The two targets are not
  interchangeable, although both express a rate.
- Markers usually allow more gain at the same target, because they
  separate sibs. The run above is not a counterexample to that, since the
  two versions met targets on different measures.
- With markers, the target can sometimes be met with fewer selected
  individuals than $1/(k\Delta F)$, by choosing individuals whose alleles
  balance each other, but most of the restriction is then spent on that
  balancing rather than on merit.

## Separate sexes

When the simulation has separate sexes, select females and males with
`nFemale` and `nMale`. Each sex then supplies half of the gametes, and the
two are ranked separately against a shared measure of fixation. The
selected females come before the males in the returned population, so a
balanced crossing plan can be built from their positions. `selectCross`
accepts the same arguments together with `restrInbr = TRUE`; setting
`nInd` instead in a simulation with sexes gives a warning, because
crosses between sexes cannot then use every parent equally.

```{r eval=FALSE}
parents = selectOC(pop, nFemale = 50, nMale = 10, simParam = SP)

# Or select and cross at random in one step
progeny = selectCross(pop, nFemale = 50, nMale = 10, nCrosses = 200,
                      restrInbr = TRUE, simParam = SP)
```

## Choosing the target

A target is easiest to choose as an effective population size,
$\Delta F = 1/(kN_e)$. An $N_e$ of 50 to 100 is often quoted as the
minimum for maintaining a population's fitness in the long term
[@toro2011Assessing], which
corresponds to $\Delta F$ between 0.01 and 0.005 for a diploid.

The target interacts with the number selected. A random set of $N$
diploids contributing equally raises the expected fixation by about
$1/(2N)$ of the remaining heterozygosity, so selecting 40 individuals at
random gives about 0.0125 on average, above the default target. A
particular set can do better or worse than that average, as the first
example showed, where the 40 best phenotypes met the default target. A
target
well below $1/(kN)$ forces the method to spend most of its effort
balancing allele frequencies, and a target the candidates cannot meet
gives a warning and returns the set found with the strongest restriction
tried. When that happens, select more individuals or relax the target.

`selectOC` selects on whatever `trait` and `use` name, so the restriction
combines with an index (see the [Selection](Selection.html) article) or
with estimated breeding values from `vignette("GenomicSelection")` or the
[Pedigree BLUP](PedigreeBLUP.html) article.
